Eliphaz and Bildad each spoke three times. Zophar spoke twice. All of their speeches are recorded as long poems.

Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar explained the reason why they thought Job was suffering. Throughout his life, Eliphaz had noticed that trouble came to foolish people. Suffering was how they were taught as well as punished for their sins. Eliphaz believed that this was a pattern for how things work in the world. He believed that it was happening in Job’s case.

Bildad had noticed that God didn’t bring judgement against people who hadn’t sinned. This was a lesson that people had taught for hundreds of years. Bildad believed it was a pattern for how things work in the world. So he thought that Job and his family were being punished for their sins.

Zophar was sure that ungodly people are always punished. He believed that this is how things had always been in the world. He was sure that God was bringing judgement on Job for sins Job had committed.

Job answered Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar each time after they spoke. Job was sad and angry because his friends said things that weren’t helpful. Many of the things they said were true. But the patterns they noticed in life didn’t apply to Job’s case. Job hadn’t sinned in secret. Job didn’t claim to have never sinned. But he knew that God wasn’t punishing him for his sins. Job knew that he had lived the way God wanted people to live. His friends didn’t understand him. They accused him falsely.

Job believed that God did understand him. Job believed that God knew that he wasn’t guilty of secret sins. Job wanted God to explain why his life had become so difficult. Job was very confused by God and angry at him. But Job continued to have respect for God and to avoid evil. He did this even though he was suffering terribly. This showed that Job had wisdom and understanding.
In this second round of speeches, Job's friends discuss the fate of wicked people. They suggest that Job's condition means he has sinned.

Job’s friends claimed they were delivering God’s message of *consolation *or comfort. But Job found no comfort in their words. He asked them to comfort him by giving him silent attention ({{Job 15:11|15:11}}; {{Job 16:2|16:2}}; {{Job 13:5|13:5}}).

- *When I think about what I am saying*: Job felt upset about his horrible task of complaining against God and talking about his terrors ({{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:15-16|15–16}}, {{Job 13:22|22}}; {{Job 23:1-5|23:1–5}}; {{Job 6:4|6:4}}; {{Job 27:20|27:20}}; {{Job 30:15|30:15}}).

- *my body trembles*: This reaction is similar to that of the prophets Habakkuk, Ezekiel, and Daniel ({{Habakkuk 1:5|Habakkuk 1:5}}; {{Habakkuk 3:16|3:16}}; {{Ezekiel 3:14|Ezekiel 3:14}}; {{Daniel 8:27|Daniel 8:27}}; {{Daniel 10:8-9|10:8–9}}).

Despite what Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar claimed, Job observed that evil people have children and grandchildren ({{Job 5:4|5:4}}); {{Job 18:19|18:19}}; {{Job 20:10|20:10}}). These should be rewards for righteous people ({{Proverbs 17:6|Proverbs 17:6}}). But Job felt they would not be his reward ({{Job 1:18-19|Job 1:18–19}}; see also {{Job 42:13-16|42:13–16}}).

*the lamp of the wicked put out*: Job disagreed with Bildad and the standard perspective of wisdom ({{Job 18:5-6|18:5–6}}, {{Job 18:18|18}}; {{Proverbs 13:9|Proverbs 13:9}}; {{Proverbs 20:20|20:20}}; {{Job 24:20|24:20}}; see God’s comments at {{Job 38:15|Job 38:15}}).

- *It is said*: Job was quoting and responding to his friends' arguments. 

- *God lays up one’s punishment for his children*: Eliphaz and Zophar said this, but Job believed God should punish the people who sin ({{Job 5:4|5:4}}; {{Job 20:10|20:10}}; see {{Ezekiel 18:19-20|Ezekiel 18:19–20}}).

- This question assumes the answer that no one can teach God a lesson ({{Isaiah 40:13-14|Isaiah 40:13–14}}; {{Isaiah 45:9|45:9}}; {{Romans 11:34|Romans 11:34}}; {{1 Corinthians 2:16|1 Corinthians 2:16}}).

- The phrase *those on high* might refer to good or bad angels (demons) ({{1 Corinthians 6:3|1 Corinthians 6:3}}; {{2 Peter 2:4|2 Peter 2:4}}; {{Jude 6|Jude 1:6}}; {{Revelation 20:1-3|Revelation 20:1–3}}). Or, more likely, it refers to powerful people on earth ({{Job 34:17-19|Job 34:17–19}}).
*his bones are rich with marrow*: People once believed bones were the source of health.
*in the bitterness of his soul*: Job often complained about how life seemed useless ({{Job 3:20|3:20}}; {{Job 7:11|7:11}}; {{Job 9:18|9:18}}; {{Job 10:1|10:1}}).
*where are the tents in which the wicked dwell*: Job was echoing the words of Bildad, Eliphaz and Zophar ({{Job 8:22|8:22}}; {{Job 15:34|15:34}}; {{Job 20:26|20:26}}).
*The clods of the valley are sweet to him*: Job considered death as a relief ({{Job 3:17-18|3:17–18}}).
They told lies about Job and God ({{Job 13:4|13:4}}; {{Job 42:7|42:7}}).
In this third round of speeches, Job's friends plainly accuse him of being evil and sharing the fate of those who do evil.

- Eliphaz did not understand that God would *delight* in Job’s right relationship with him, just as God does with every *righteous* person ({{Job 1:8|1:8}}; {{Job 2:3|2:3}}; {{1 Chronicles 29:17|1 Chronicles 29:17}}; {{Psalm 147:10-11|Psalms 147:10–11}}; {{Proverbs 11:1|Proverbs 11:1}}, {{Proverbs 11:20|20}}; {{Proverbs 12:22|12:22}}). God would also* benefit* from Job’s steady faith, which exposed the lie in Satan’s challenge ({{Job 1:9-12|Job 1:9–12}}; {{Job 2:4-6|2:4–6}}).

- Job firmly claimed that he was *blameless* ({{Job 23:10-12|23:10–12}}). God said the same thing ({{Job 1:1|1:1}}, {{Job 1:8|8}}; {{Job 2:3|2:3}}).

The law and prophets forbade taking clothing as *security* for loans ({{Exodus 22:26-27|Exodus 22:26–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:10-13|Deuteronomy 24:10–13}}; {{Ezekiel 18:7-8|Ezekiel 18:7–8}}; {{Amos 2:8|Amos 2:8}}). In contrast, Job gave clothing to poor people ({{Job 31:19-20|Job 31:19–20}}).

The Old Testament assigns Israel the duty of caring for *widows* and *the fatherless* ({{Deuteronomy 10:18|Deuteronomy 10:18}}; {{Deuteronomy 14:29|14:29}}). It often condemns neglecting them as the worst evil against society ({{Exodus 22:22-24|Exodus 22:22–24}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:19|Deuteronomy 27:19}}). Job agreed that neglecting them was wrong but claimed he was innocent ({{Job 24:3|Job 24:3}}, {{Job 24:21|21}}; {{Job 29:12-13|29:12–13}}; {{Job 31:16-18|31:16–18}}, {{Job 31:21|21}}).
*What does God know?*: Job did not claim that God cannot see, but others have (see {{Psalm 10:11|Psalms 10:11}}; {{Psalm 73:11|73:11}}; {{Psalm 94:7|94:7}}).
*so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked*: Eliphaz repeated Job’s words to him ({{Job 21:16|21:16b}}).

*The righteous see it and are glad*: Those in a right relationship with God will be *glad* to *see* justice done and wrong things made right (see also {{Psalm 58:10-11|Psalm 58:10–11}}; {{Revelation 19:1-4|Revelation 19:1–4}}). Eliphaz's perspective overlooked God's wish "that the wicked should turn from their ways and live" (see {{Ezekiel 33:11|Ezekiel 33:11}}).

- The term *instruction* (Hebrew *torah*, also meaning "law," {{Deuteronomy 17:11|Deuteronomy 17:11}}), used in Job only here, often refers to the "Pentateuch" (Genesis through Deuteronomy). 

- *Receive … lay up*: See {{Deuteronomy 4:1-2|Deuteronomy 4:1–2}}; {{Deuteronomy 6:6-9|6:6–9}}; {{Psalm 119:11|Psalm 119:11}}; {{Proverbs 2:1-9|Proverbs 2:1–9}}. Job had done this thing ({{Job 23:12|Job 23:12}}).

*return to the Almighty*: Bildad and Zophar had already made a wrong application of this principle of the Bible ({{Job 8:5-6|8:5–6}}; {{Job 11:13-14|11:13–14}}; {{Isaiah 55:6-7|Isaiah 55:6–7}}; {{Hosea 14:1-2|Hosea 14:1–2}}; {{Zechariah 1:3|Zechariah 1:3}}; {{Acts 26:20|Acts 26:20}}). Now Eliphaz also makes a wrong application of it.

*gold of Ophir: Ophir* was probably in southern Arabia (see {{1 Kings 9:28|1 Kings 9:28}}; {{1 Kings 22:48|22:48}}). The *gold of Ophir* set the standard for fine gold ({{Isaiah 13:12|Isaiah 13:12}}). Queens wore it at weddings ({{Psalm 45:9|Psalm 45:9}}).

God promises to be a "treasure" for his people ({{Psalm 16:5|Psalm 16:5}}; {{Isaiah 33:6|Isaiah 33:6}}; {{Matthew 19:21|Matthew 19:21}}; {{Mark 10:21|Mark 10:21}}). Even if they own nothing, they will be "rich" ({{2 Corinthians 6:10|2 Corinthians 6:10}}; {{James 2:5|James 2:5}}).

- Ironically, Job will pray, God will hear, and Eliphaz will benefit ({{Job 42:8|42:8}}).

- *you will fulfill your vows*: People often vowed after God forgave them ({{Hosea 14:2|Hosea 14:2}}; {{Jonah 1:16|Jonah 1:16}}; {{Jonah 2:9|2:9}}). They also vowed when asking help from God ({{Judges 11:29-40|Judges 11:29–40}}; {{1 Samuel 1:1-28|1 Samuel 1:1–28}}). *Vows* mean a serious commitments or to swear a promise ({{Numbers 30:2|Numbers 30:2}}; {{Deuteronomy 23:23|Deuteronomy 23:23}}; {{Psalm 22:25|Psalms 22:25}}; {{Psalm 61:5|61:5}}, {{Psalm 61:8|8}}; {{Psalm 116:14|116:14}}, {{Psalm 116:18|18}}; {{Ecclesiastes 5:4-5|Ecclesiastes 5:4–5}}).

This difficult text probably shows how effective the prayer of a person in a right relationship with God can be. The idea appears throughout the Bible ({{Psalm 34:15|Psalms 34:15}}, {{Psalm 34:17|17}}; {{Psalm 145:18|145:18}}; {{Proverbs 15:8|Proverbs 15:8}}, {{Job 15:29|29}}; {{James 5:16|James 5:16}}; see also {{Genesis 18:23-32|Genesis 18:23–32}}; {{Genesis 19:29|19:29}}; {{Genesis 20:7|20:7}}, {{Genesis 20:17|17}}; {{Genesis 32:28|32:28}}; {{Exodus 9:28-32|Exodus 9:28–32}}; {{Exodus 17:11|17:11}}; {{Exodus 32:10-14|32:10–14}}; {{Romans 5:19|Romans 5:19}}).
Job released his earlier doubts ({{Job 9:14-20|9:14–20}}, {{Job 9:32|32}}). Now he expresses confidence that he could present his *complaint* to God with success.

*plead my case*: Job wanted to present his legal *case* to God ({{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:18|18}}, {{Job 13:22|22}}; {{Job 16:21|16:21}}; {{Job 31:35|31:35}}). Abraham pleaded directly with God about Sodom ({{Genesis 18:25-32|Genesis 18:25–32}}). Moses did the same for Israel ({{Exodus 32:12-13|Exodus 32:12–13}}; {{Numbers 14:13-19|Numbers 14:13–19}}).

- Earlier, Job thought God was too powerful for him to "summon" ({{Job 9:19|9:19}}). He asked for "a mediator" and requested that God not "frighten" him ({{Job 9:33-34|9:33–34}}; {{Job 13:21|13:21}}). Here, he showed more hope that God would give him a fair legal hearing. 

- *delivered*: Job wanted God to declare him innocent, not forgive him as if he were guilty ({{Job 13:18|13:18}}; see {{Psalm 17:2-3|Psalms 17:2–3}}; {{Psalm 26:1-3|26:1–3}}).

*has tested *me: Job did not want the kind of punishment that would make him clean as through "a refiner’s fire" ({{Proverbs 17:3|Proverbs 17:3}}; {{Zechariah 13:9|Zechariah 13:9}}; {{Malachi 3:2-3|Malachi 3:2–3}}). He wanted a test to show he was already as pure *as gold* and did not need to change his life ({{Job 22:23|Job 22:23}}).

- *Terrified in His presence*: See {{Psalm 77:3|Psalms 77:3}}; {{Psalm 88:16|88:16}}; {{Psalm 119:120|119:120}}.

- Job had earlier complained about being in *darkness* ({{Job 19:8|Job 19:8}}). Eliphaz and Bildad said this fate is for the evil person ({{Job 15:22|15:22}}; {{Job 22:1|22:1}}; {{Job 18:6|18:6}}, {{Job 18:18|18}}).

*reserve times*: God sets times for *judgment* ({{Ecclesiastes 3:17|Ecclesiastes 3:17}}; {{Ecclesiastes 8:6|8:6}}; {{Daniel 2:21|Daniel 2:21}}; {{Luke 21:22-24|Luke 21:22–24}}). But we do not know when they are ({{Acts 1:7|Acts 1:7}}). He will reveal them at the right time ({{1 Thessalonians 5:1-28|1 Thessalonians 5:1–28}}; {{1 Timothy 6:15|1 Timothy 6:15}}).

The books of the law, wisdom literature, and prophecy all condemned moving markers of boundaries ({{Deuteronomy 19:14|Deuteronomy 19:14}}; {{Deuteronomy 27:17|27:17}}; {{Proverbs 22:28|Proverbs 22:28}}; {{Proverbs 23:10|23:10}}; see study note on Hosea 5:10).
This list of criminal behaviors first emphasizes crimes against weak people ({{Job 24:2-12|24:2–12}}). Then it examines the criminals themselves ({{Job 24:13-17|24:13–17}}).

The law prohibited taking essential possessions as security or a down payment for a loan ({{Job 22:6-9|22:6–9}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:6|Deuteronomy 24:6}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:10-13|10–13}}, {{Deuteronomy 24:17-21|17–21}}).

*glean the vineyards of the wicked*: Job described the desperate situation of poor people. If someone stole their fields like in the case of Naboth's vineyard, the poor person would harvest for the thieves instead of for themselves ({{Job 24:2|24:2}}; see {{1 Kings 21:1-29|1 Kings 21:1–29}}). They would only get the bits that remained. If the poor had to *glean* from *fields* of the *wicked* people, they would receive nothing ({{Leviticus 19:10|Leviticus 19:10}}; {{Leviticus 23:22|23:22}}). But if they would try to *gather *from the fields of just people, they would be something left for them ({{Leviticus 19:9-10|Leviticus 19:9–10}}; {{Leviticus 23:22|23:22}}; {{Ruth 2:1-23|Ruth 2:1–23}}).

Those who did not lend fairly sometimes took the clothing or blankets of those in debt as a security for the loan. This left those in debt without proper clothing or covering ({{Job 22:6|22:6}}; {{Exodus 22:26-27|Exodus 22:26–27}}; {{Deuteronomy 24:11-13|Deuteronomy 24:11–13}}; {{Amos 2:8|Amos 2:8}}).
*the nursing child of the poor is seized for a debt*: See {{2 Kings 4:1|2 Kings 4:1}}; {{Nehemiah 5:1-5|Nehemiah 5:1–5}}; {{Matthew 18:25|Matthew 18:25}}.

Forcing workers to *tread the winepresses* while they *go thirsty* violates the principle of letting workers enjoy some of the produce they are harvesting (see {{Deuteronomy 25:4|Deuteronomy 25:4}}; compare {{2 Timothy 2:6|2 Timothy 2:6}}).

*yet God charges no one with wrongdoing*: Job thought that, unlike God's usual character, God did not help those treated wrong or stop evil people from hurting their victims ({{Exodus 2:23-24|Exodus 2:23–24}}; {{Psalm 12:5|Psalm 12:5}}; {{Job 24:2-12|Job 24:2–12}}; {{Job 24:13-17|24:13–17}}).

These ideas seem to go against Job's observations. Some scholars think Bildad or Zophar might have said them. However, Job might have been speaking against evil people, making fun of his friends' opinions by quoting them. Or he might have meant that the fate of evil people also affects those in a right relationship with God. His friends described this earlier ({{Job 5:2-7|5:2–7}}; {{Job 15:17-25|15:17–25}}; {{Job 8:8-19|8:8–19}}; {{Job 18:5-21|18:5–21}}; {{Job 20:4-29|20:4–29}}; {{Job 21:23-26|21:23–26}}).

Eliphaz stated that being innocent or pure is almost impossible ({{Job 4:17-19|4:17–19}}; {{Job 15:14-16|15:14–16}}). A person can achieve it only after suffering ({{Job 22:21-23|22:21–23}}). Bildad argued that only those who are completely blameless can hope to be pure ({{Job 8:20|8:20}}).

Job’s friends did not help him ({{Job 12:2|12:2}}; {{Job 16:4|16:4}}). Bildad's claim that innocence was impossible upset Job deeply ({{Job 10:1-7|10:1–7}}; {{Job 13:3|13:3}}, {{Job 13:13-19|13–19}}; {{Job 16:18-21|16:18–21}}; {{Job 19:23-27|19:23–27}}; {{Job 23:2-7|23:2–7}}).

Eliphaz, Zophar, and Elihu all claimed that the right *spirit* was guiding them ({{Job 4:15|4:15}}; {{Job 20:3|20:3}}; {{Job 32:18|32:18}}; {{Job 33:4|33:4}}; see also {{Jeremiah 29:8-9|Jeremiah 29:8–9}}; {{1 Corinthians 12:10|1 Corinthians 12:10}}; {{1 John 4:1|1 John 4:1}}).

- The Hebrew word,* Sheol,* is where all dead people go. It is *beneath the waters*.

- The Hebrew word,* Abaddon,* is the place where evil people go to their destruction.

The Hebrew word *tsapon* means *north.* It sometimes refers to the northern mountain of the Canaanite gods, similar to Mount Olympus ({{Genesis 13:14|Genesis 13:14}}). The Berean Standard Bible refers to it as the sky, stretched *over empty space* (see {{Genesis 1:6-8|Genesis 1:6–8}}; {{Psalm 104:2-3|Psalm 104:2–3}}; {{Isaiah 40:22-23|Isaiah 40:22–23}}).

People once believed that mountains at the edge of the horizon were the *foundations* or "pillars" of heaven or the earth ({{Judges 16:25-26|Judges 16:25–26;}} {{Job 9:6|Job 9:6}}). They thought these mountains extended from beneath the sea's waters up to the clouds, supporting the dome of the heavens ({{Jonah 2:6|Jonah 2:6}}).

- *He stirred the sea* (compare {{Exodus 14:21|Exodus 14:21}}; {{Mark 4:39|Mark 4:39}}; compare {{Isaiah 51:15|Isaiah 51:15}}; {{Jeremiah 31:35|Jeremiah 31:35}}). God performed a miracle for his people. 

- *He shattered Rahab*: God showed control over the sea symbolized as a monster ("Rahab"), challenging myths about the sea being divine. See also {{Psalm 74:13-14|Psalms 74:13–14}}; {{Psalm 89:9-10|89:9–10}}; {{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; {{Isaiah 51:9-10|51:9–10}}.

- *His breath* (or *wind*): God's authority clears *the skies* after a storm ({{Job 26:12|26:12}}). 

- *The fleeing serpent* relates to "Yam" and "Rahab" (see study note on 7:12). It provides background for the image of Satan as a "dragon" ({{Isaiah 27:1|Isaiah 27:1}}; also {{Psalm 74:13-14|Psalm 74:13–14}}; see {{Genesis 3:15|Genesis 3:15}}; {{Romans 16:20|Romans 16:20}}; {{Revelation 12:9|Revelation 12:9}}; {{Revelation 20:2|20:2}}).
*Job continued his discourse*: He no longer responded to his three friends. Instead, he returned to the themes of his opening statement ({{Job 3:1-26|3:1–26}}).

- The Bible allows for making a vow to the living God ({{Ruth 3:13|Ruth 3:13}}; {{1 Samuel 20:21|1 Samuel 20:21}}; {{1 Samuel 25:26|25:26}}; {{1 Kings 17:1|1 Kings 17:1}}; {{1 Kings 18:15|18:15}}; {{Jeremiah 4:2|Jeremiah 4:2}}). But sometimes people make silly or false vows ({{1 Samuel 14:39|1 Samuel 14:39}}, {{1 Samuel 14:45|45}}; {{Jeremiah 5:2|Jeremiah 5:2}}). 

- Elihu later criticized Job for claiming that God *deprived me of justice* ({{Job 34:5|Job 34:5}}).

- *embittered my soul* ({{Job 7:11|7:11}}; {{Job 10:1|10:1}}; {{Job 21:25|21:25}}): Compare Naomi and the widow from Shunem after losing her son ({{Ruth 1:20-21|Ruth 1:20–21}}; {{2 Kings 4:27|2 Kings 4:27}}).

Job found it wrong and offensive to admit that his friends were correct. It was a terrible act to condemn an innocent man like him ({{Exodus 23:7|Exodus 23:7}}; {{Proverbs 6:16-19|Proverbs 6:16–19}}; {{Proverbs 17:15|17:15}}).
Some interpreters think this is a new speech by Zophar. Without it, Zophar has no speech in this cycle.

This section is an isolated speech. There is no speaker listed, so it might continue from earlier words. Some see it as a creative summary by the author of Job. It emphasizes the limits of human wisdom and sets the stage for the Lord's speeches.
People who mined would melt rock by burning a *fire* in a mine for days or weeks to extract the solid matter (ore). Some used *fire* and then cold water to crack the rocks.
Wisdom does not come from people. God is the true source of wisdom ({{Job 28:23-28|28:23–28}}).
The metals, gems, and glass listed here were valuable in the ancient world. However, the speaker says wisdom is more valuable than wealth.

When God looks across the entire earth, he sees his wisdom in his creation ({{Job 28:23|28:23}}). God later showed his wisdom to Job by taking him on a tour of the universe (chapters {{Job 38:1-41:34|38–41}}).
*the fear of the Lord *(Hebrew, *’adonay*): In the book of Job, this name for God appears only here. This might suggest that chapter {{Job 28:1-28|28}} is a poem by the person narrating.

Job compares his past happiness, honor, and wealth with his current loss of social dignity and divine friendship (chapters {{Job 29:1-25|29}}and {{Job 30:1-31|30}}). He ends his speech with broad vows of innocence (chapter {{Job 31:1-40|31}}).

In other parts of the text, Job uses the Hebrew word *shamar* to describe what he sees as God's severe surveillance ({{Job 10:14|10:14}}; {{Job 13:27|13:27}}; {{Job 14:16|14:16}}). However, here it refers to God's kind care, meaning *watched over* ({{Psalm 121:3-8|Psalm 121:3–8}}).
*The city gate *served as the town's administrative center (see {{Ruth 4:1-2|Ruth 4:1–2}}, {{Ruth 4:11|11}}).

Job described his *righteousness* using royal imagery. In the Bible, a *robe* often symbolizes *righteousness* ({{Psalm 132:9|Psalm 132:9}}; {{Isaiah 59:17|Isaiah 59:17}}; {{Isaiah 61:10|Isaiah 61:10}}; {{Romans 13:14|Romans 13:14}}; {{Revelation 19:8|Revelation 19:8}}).
Job was active in searching out and helping strangers in need.

*and multiply my days as the sand* (literally *after I have counted my days like sand*): Job believed the length of his years showed God's blessing. This was similar to the numerous people descended from Abraham or the abundance of supplies Joseph had in Egypt ({{Genesis 15:5|Genesis 15:5}}; {{Genesis 32:12|32:12}}; {{Genesis 41:49|Genesis 41:49}}).

In the past, Job was a *comforter of the mourners* ({{Job 4:3-4|4:3–4}}). This verse is a prophetic command closely linked to the work of the Christ ({{Isaiah 40:1|Isaiah 40:1}}; {{Isaiah 61:1-3|61:1–3}}; {{Luke 4:18-19|Luke 4:18–19}}; see also {{2 Corinthians 1:3-4|2 Corinthians 1:3–4}}).

In the past, the most important members of society praised Job ({{Job 29:11|29:11}}). Now, the least important made fun of him and spit in his face ({{Job 30:1|30:1,}}{{Job 30:10|10}}). Compare with {{Psalm 35:15|Psalms 35:15}}; {{Psalm 69:12|69:12}}; {{Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65}}; {{Mark 15:17-20|15:17–20}}.

They live in scary valleys (*wadis*), caves (*holes*), and among *rocks*. 

The miserable life of those making fun of Job was like: 

- Israel’s situation under Midianite abuse ({{Judges 6:2|Judges 6:2}}).

- David’s life when he fled from King Saul ({{1 Samuel 22:1-2|1 Samuel 22:1–2}}).

- The prophet Elijah’s life as he waited for the Lord’s instruction ({{1 Kings 17:3-8|1 Kings 17:3–8}}).
*they mock me*: See also {{Job 17:6|17:6}}; compare with {{Psalm 69:12|Psalm 69:12}}; {{Lamentations 3:14|Lamentations 3:14}}, {{Lamentations 3:63|63}}.

- *keep far from me*: See also {{Job 19:13-15|19:13–15}}; compare {{Psalm 88:8|Psalm 88:8}}; {{Proverbs 19:7|Proverbs 19:7}}; {{Matthew 26:56|Matthew 26:56}}.

- Spitting in someone's face showed extreme dislike or hatred ({{Deuteronomy 25:9|Deuteronomy 25:9}}; {{Isaiah 50:6|Isaiah 50:6}}; {{Matthew 26:67|Matthew 26:67}}; {{Matthew 27:30|27:30}}; {{Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65}}).

- The series of images here shows a military attack on a city with strong defenses. Job had already used this image to describe God's attack on him ({{Job 19:10-12|Job 19:10–12}}).

- The word translated as *snares* might refer to ramps raised against a city's walls. A siege ramp was a large sloped structure of earth and stones that armies built against city walls. These ramps allowed attacking soldiers to climb up to the top of the walls during a battle.
*He seizes me by the collar*: The Hebrew in this verse is hard to translate. It might mean Job feels like God is choking him and he is a throw him into the mud (compare {{Job 30:19|30:19}}).
*dust and ashes*: Earlier, Job sat among the *ashes* in pain ({{Job 2:8|2:8}}). Later, he would sit in *dust and ashes* to "repent" ({{Job 42:6|42:6}}).
*You do not answer*: Job often complained about this ({{Job 9:16|9:16}}; {{Job 19:7|19:7}}; {{Job 23:2-9|23:2–9}}; {{Job 31:35|31:35}}). But God soon responded ({{Job 38:1|38:1}}).

Job felt like he was caught in a storm and blown around like useless "straw" or "chaff" ({{Job 9:17|9:17}}; {{Job 21:18|21:18}}; {{Job 27:21|27:21}}; {{Psalm 1:4|Psalm 1:4}}; {{Isaiah 17:13|Isaiah 17:13}}).
Before his testing began, people respected Job in the public square ({{Job 29:7-10|29:7–10}}, {{Job 29:21-25|21–25}}). He helped those in need ({{Job 29:11-17|29:11–17}}).

Job might have been expressing how he saw himself, how others saw him, or both. By saying he was *a brother of jackals, a companion to owls,* Job might have been describing his deep grief ({{Micah 1:8|Micah 1:8}}). People associated *jackals* with things devastated or ruins (see {{Psalm 63:10|Psalm 63:10}}; {{Isaiah 13:22|Isaiah 13:22}}; {{Isaiah 34:13|34:13}}; {{Isaiah 35:7|35:7}}; {{Jeremiah 9:11|Jeremiah 9:11}}; {{Jeremiah 10:22|10:22}}; {{Jeremiah 49:33|49:33}}; {{Jeremiah 51:37|51:37}}; {{Lamentations 5:18|Lamentations 5:18}}; {{Ezekiel 13:4|Ezekiel 13:4}}; {{Malachi 1:3|Malachi 1:3}}).
People with a comfortable life had skin protected from the sun and wind. Dark skin suggested physical and social decline ({{Lamentations 4:8|Lamentations 4:8}}; {{Lamentations 5:10|5:10}}).
